notes.A: Lysine is incorporated into proteins and is not the substrate for iNOS-mediated nitric oxide formation.
notes.B: Histidine can be decarboxylated to histamine, which is a distinct inflammatory mediator from nitric oxide.
notes.C: Tyrosine is used in catecholamine and thyroid hormone pathways rather than as the iNOS substrate.
notes.E: Proline is abundant in collagen and can be metabolised through different reactions from nitric oxide synthesis.

questions.stem: Which enzyme kills some bacteria by cleaving peptidoglycan bonds?
questions.why: Lysozyme hydrolyses a glycosidic bond in bacterial peptidoglycan, weakening the wall of susceptible bacteria. It therefore provides an oxygen-independent mechanism of antimicrobial defence.

notes.A: Perforin facilitates granzyme delivery into target cells rather than cutting the bacterial peptidoglycan backbone.
notes.B: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide, which is a redox reaction rather than cleavage of a cell-wall polysaccharide.
notes.D: Elastase is a protease and cleaves proteins rather than hydrolysing the peptidoglycan glycan backbone.
notes.E: Caspases are proteases involved in pathways such as apoptosis and inflammation, rather than bacterial wall hydrolases.

questions.stem: An immunogen differs from a non-immunogenic antigen because an immunogen can:

options.label: E
options.text: Cause immediate cell lysis without exposure

questions.why: An antigen can bind a specific antibody or receptor. An immunogen also elicits a specific immune response in the host, so its defining property is induction rather than binding alone.

notes.B: Fc receptors recognise antibody constant regions, but Fc binding does not define the ability to induce an immune response.
notes.C: Specific antibody production requires B-lineage cells, which differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
notes.D: Complement can bind or be recruited to some targets, but that interaction alone does not establish specific immunogenicity.
notes.E: Immediate lysis is an effector outcome, whereas immunogenicity describes induction of a specific response after exposure.

questions.stem: A small drug molecule binds antibody but elicits little response until linked to a protein. The molecule is a:
questions.why: A hapten is small enough to be recognised by a specific antibody but usually cannot elicit an effective response on its own. Attachment to an immunogenic carrier can supply the needed context.

notes.A: A mitogen drives proliferation of many lymphocytes and is not defined by a need for a carrier protein.
notes.B: A toxoid is an inactivated toxin that retains antigenic properties, rather than a small carrier-dependent determinant.
notes.C: An adjuvant enhances responses to an antigen but is not the small molecule that binds the specific antibody in this stem.
notes.D: An alloantigen differs between members of the same species and does not necessarily require attachment to a carrier.

questions.stem: Which term describes the part of an antigen bound by an antibody?
questions.why: The epitope is the particular region or molecular feature of an antigen recognised by an antibody. The complementary binding surface is the antibody's paratope.

notes.A: The paratope lies on the antibody and binds the determinant on the antigen.
notes.C: Isotype identifies immunoglobulin classes or subclasses through differences in constant regions.
notes.D: An idiotype is the set of distinctive antigenic features associated with an antibody's variable regions.
notes.E: An allotype is an inherited allelic variant of an immunoglobulin, rather than the target feature bound by it.

questions.stem: What is the name of the antigen-binding region on an immunoglobulin?
questions.why: The paratope is the antigen-binding surface of an antibody, formed mainly by loops in its heavy- and light-chain variable regions. It contacts the corresponding epitope.

notes.A: The epitope is the recognised determinant on the antigen, opposite the antibody surface that binds it.
notes.B: A hapten is a small antigenic molecule that can bind antibody, rather than part of the immunoglobulin.
notes.C: An adjuvant enhances an immune response to an antigen and does not make up the antibody binding site.
notes.E: An immunoglobulin allotype is an inherited variant, rather than the surface that makes direct antigen contact.

questions.stem: Antibody binding lost when a native protein unfolds most strongly suggests recognition of a:
questions.why: A conformational epitope depends on the protein's folded shape, which can bring distant residues together. Unfolding can separate those residues and abolish recognition even when the sequence remains intact.

notes.A: A linear epitope comprises contiguous residues and can often remain available after the protein unfolds.
notes.B: A free amino acid does not account for recognition of a surface created by the folding of a native protein.
notes.D: The antibody's heavy-chain constant region controls effector properties rather than defining the folded site on the antigen.
notes.E: An isolated phosphate group alone would not explain the dependence on the protein's native three-dimensional arrangement.

questions.stem: Conventional CD4 T cells chiefly recognize peptides displayed by which molecules?
questions.why: Conventional CD4 T cells use their antigen receptors to recognise peptides on MHC class II. Their CD4 coreceptor binds class II, which is expressed by professional antigen-presenting cells.

notes.B: Peptide presentation on MHC class I is chiefly recognised by CD8 cells rather than conventional CD4 helper T cells.
notes.C: Secretory IgA binds mucosal antigens as an antibody and does not display peptides to CD4 T cells.
notes.D: Surface IgE may be bound to Fc receptors, but it is not a peptide-presenting molecule.
notes.E: C3b acts mainly as an opsonin and complement component rather than directly presenting peptide to CD4 cells.

questions.stem: A nucleated cell presents cytosolic viral peptides to CD8 T cells using which molecules?
questions.why: MHC class I on nucleated cells can display peptides derived from cytosolic proteins. CD8 T cells recognise appropriate peptide–class I complexes and can respond to infected cells.

notes.A: MHC class II is mainly used by professional antigen-presenting cells to display peptides to CD4 T cells.
notes.B: Surface IgD serves as a B-cell receptor and does not present cytosolic peptides to CD8 cells.
notes.C: C5b initiates assembly of terminal complement, rather than acting as a peptide display molecule.
notes.D: IgM binds antigen as an antibody and does not present processed peptides for CD8 recognition.

questions.stem: ABO blood-group differences between members of one species are examples of:
questions.why: ABO antigen structures vary between individuals within the human species. A person can therefore recognise an ABO determinant from another individual as an alloantigen.

notes.A: An autoantigen is a constituent of the individual's own body, rather than a differing antigen from another human.
notes.C: A xenoantigen is derived from a different species, whereas ABO differences occur within humans.
notes.D: A hapten is a small antigenic compound with limited immunogenicity alone, not a term for inherited blood-group differences.
notes.E: A tolerogen induces immune tolerance, rather than naming the between-person origin of an ABO antigen.

questions.stem: A polysaccharide antigen stimulates B cells without T-helper contact. Which response is typical?

options.label: C
options.text: Direct recognition by peptide MHC I

questions.why: Some polysaccharides activate B cells through repeated epitopes without conventional cognate T-cell help. The response is often largely IgM, with less affinity maturation and durable memory than a T-dependent response.

notes.A: Strong germinal-centre switching generally needs cognate T-cell help, which is absent from the situation described.
notes.B: A polysaccharide acting on B cells does not usually generate the dominant CD8 T-cell expansion listed here.
notes.C: MHC class I displays peptides rather than directly presenting intact polysaccharide to a B-cell receptor.
notes.E: Follicular helper T cells support T-dependent germinal centres, whereas these polysaccharides can stimulate B cells without that contact.

questions.stem: What explains cross-reactivity between an antibody and two different antigens?
questions.why: An antibody remains specific for molecular features rather than for an entire antigen. Two distinct antigens can therefore bind the same antibody if they share sufficiently similar epitopes.

notes.A: Cross-reactivity can occur despite specificity, because both antigens can share features recognised by the same binding site.
notes.B: Heavy-chain identity alone does not explain why two antigens bind, because the relevant similarity is between their epitopes.
notes.D: Typical antigen recognition is mediated by variable regions, while Fc binds effector molecules and receptors.
notes.E: Variable-region residues create the paratope and are generally needed for specific binding to shared determinants.

questions.stem: What is the principal role of an adjuvant in a vaccine?
questions.why: A vaccine adjuvant changes the context in which the immune system sees the antigen. It can enhance innate activation and antigen presentation, leading to a stronger or more durable adaptive response.

notes.B: The antigen provides the target specificity and remains necessary even when an adjuvant improves the response.
notes.C: Many adjuvants support dendritic-cell activation or function rather than preventing their maturation.
notes.D: Increased antigen-specific B-cell activation is often an intended outcome rather than something the adjuvant blocks.
notes.E: Many adjuvants enhance local innate signals that support adaptive priming instead of broadly suppressing them.

questions.stem: Bacterial superantigens can provoke systemic cytokine release by binding directly to:
questions.why: A superantigen can link MHC class II on an antigen-presenting cell to particular T-cell receptor variable regions outside ordinary peptide-specific recognition. Many T cells can then become activated together.

notes.A: Surface IgM is a B-cell receptor, whereas these superantigens activate T cells through MHC class II and a T-cell receptor.
notes.B: CD19 is associated with B-cell signalling and C3 is a complement protein, rather than partners in this T-cell activation.
notes.C: CD14 helps detect LPS and albumin is a carrier protein, neither forming the classic superantigen bridge.
notes.D: CD16 binds IgG Fc and surface IgD is a B-cell receptor, rather than the pair that links antigen-presenting and T cells.

questions.stem: Which cell is primarily responsible for secreting large amounts of antigen-specific antibody?
questions.why: A plasma cell is a differentiated B-lineage cell with extensive machinery for protein synthesis. It secretes large quantities of immunoglobulin carrying the specificity selected during B-cell activation.

notes.A: Dendritic cells present antigen and provide costimulation, rather than secreting large amounts of antigen-specific antibody.
notes.C: Neutrophils phagocytose microbes and release antimicrobial products, but are not antibody-secreting cells.
notes.D: Natural killer cells can kill targets via Fc receptors and cytotoxic granules but do not make those antibodies.
notes.E: Cytotoxic T cells use antigen receptors to recognise and kill targets, rather than differentiating into antibody-secreting plasma cells.

questions.stem: How many polypeptide chains form the basic immunoglobulin monomer?
questions.why: A basic immunoglobulin unit contains two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains, linked by disulphide bonds. The paired variable regions create two antigen-binding arms.

notes.A: Two chains would describe one heavy–light pair and omit the second arm of the immunoglobulin unit.
notes.B: Two chains account for a single heavy–light pair, whereas the antibody unit has two such pairs.
notes.C: A J chain can associate with some polymeric antibody forms but is not a fifth chain of the basic monomer.
notes.D: Six chains exceeds the four in the two matched heavy–light pairs of a basic antibody unit.

questions.stem: What determines whether an antibody is IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD or IgE?
questions.why: The heavy-chain constant region specifies immunoglobulin class and influences its effector functions. B cells can replace that region during class switching while retaining their antigen-binding variable regions.

notes.A: The light-chain variable region contributes to antigen recognition rather than defining the immunoglobulin class.
notes.B: The epitope determines what the antibody binds, while its class is determined by the antibody's own heavy chain.
notes.D: Disulphide bonds stabilise antibody structure, but the number on light chains does not set the antibody class.
notes.E: An antigen can be a protein or other molecule, and its sequence does not directly determine the heavy-chain isotype.

questions.stem: Which two types of immunoglobulin light chains occur in humans?
questions.why: Human immunoglobulins use either kappa or lambda light chains. The two light chains in one basic antibody are of the same type, independently of its heavy-chain class.

notes.B: Alpha and gamma are heavy-chain classes associated with IgA and IgG rather than light-chain types.
notes.C: Mu and delta are heavy chains defining IgM and IgD respectively, not alternative light chains.
notes.D: Alpha is the heavy chain of IgA, and epsilon is the heavy chain of IgE.
notes.E: Gamma and epsilon are constant-region types of IgG and IgE heavy chains respectively.

questions.stem: Which portions of antibody heavy and light chains form the combining site?
questions.why: The heavy- and light-chain variable domains meet at the end of each antibody arm. Their exposed complementarity-determining loops together form most of the surface that recognises an epitope.

notes.A: Constant regions support antibody structure and effector properties rather than providing the principal antigen-contacts.
notes.B: The Fc consists of heavy-chain constant domains that can recruit effector systems rather than binding the specific epitope.
notes.C: Hinge disulphides connect heavy chains and support arm flexibility near the centre of the antibody.
notes.E: Tailpieces can contribute to polymeric antibody assembly but are remote from the antigen-binding site.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of the antibody hinge region?
questions.why: The hinge lets the two Fab arms alter their angle and spacing relative to Fc. This flexibility helps them contact epitopes that are separated by different distances.

notes.A: MHC class II recognition is a function of peptide-specific T-cell receptors rather than the antibody hinge.
notes.C: Complement factors are produced by host cells, and the hinge is a structural antibody segment rather than a secretory apparatus.
notes.D: Antibody hinges allow conformational movement and generally do not catalyse peptide hydrolysis.
notes.E: Plasma-cell maturation is a B-lineage differentiation process, separate from an antibody's structural flexibility.

questions.stem: The hypervariable loops that most directly contact antigen are called:
questions.why: Complementarity-determining regions are the variable-domain loops that form much of an antibody's contact surface. Adjacent framework residues hold the loops in position, although some also contribute to binding.

notes.A: Framework regions provide the structural scaffold around the more variable loops that usually make most antigen contacts.
notes.B: Heavy-chain constant regions determine antibody class and help recruit effector systems rather than forming the hypervariable loops.
notes.C: The secretory component is retained from a transport receptor associated with mucosal antibodies and is not an antigen-binding loop.
notes.D: Hinge segments provide flexibility between the Fab and Fc portions, away from the loops at each arm tip.

questions.stem: Which fragment of IgG retains antigen binding after papain digestion?
questions.why: Papain cleavage of IgG separates the two antigen-binding arms as individual Fab fragments. Each Fab retains one combining site, while the detached Fc region lacks those variable domains.

notes.A: Fc contains heavy-chain constant regions for effector interactions and has no specific antigen-combining site.
notes.B: C3b is a complement opsonin generated from C3, rather than a product of immunoglobulin cleavage.
notes.D: C1q is a recognition component of the classical complement pathway rather than an IgG fragment.
notes.E: The J chain helps assemble polymeric IgM and IgA and is not an antigen-binding fragment of IgG.

questions.stem: Which fragment is typically produced by pepsin digestion of IgG and retains two binding sites?
questions.why: Pepsin cleaves IgG so that the two Fab arms remain connected through the hinge as an F(ab′)₂ fragment. The resulting fragment retains two antigen-binding sites.

notes.B: An isolated Fab has only one binding site, whereas this fragment retains both connected arms.
notes.C: Fc contains constant domains rather than the two variable-region binding sites, and much of it is degraded.
notes.D: Fc gamma receptors are cellular receptors for IgG, not proteolytic fragments of the antibody.
notes.E: C3b is produced by cleavage of complement C3 rather than by pepsin acting on IgG.

questions.stem: Which antibody region mediates binding to many Fc receptors and complement proteins?
questions.why: The Fc portion consists of heavy-chain constant regions outside the antigen-binding arms. It links antigen recognition to effector responses by interacting with Fc receptors and, for suitable isotypes, complement.

notes.A: Fab contains the specific antigen-binding site rather than the main Fc receptor or C1q-binding surfaces.
notes.B: CDR3 is an antigen-contact loop within a variable region and does not mediate typical Fc interactions.
notes.C: The light-chain variable domain helps form the paratope and is absent from the Fc portion.
notes.E: The paratope binds the antigen's epitope, while Fc provides the separate interface with effector molecules.

questions.stem: Which antibody class is transported across the human placenta to provide passive neonatal protection?
questions.why: The neonatal Fc receptor moves maternal IgG across the placenta and releases it into fetal circulation. It gives temporary systemic protection without requiring the fetus to make that antibody.

notes.A: Secretory IgA is transferred mainly in breast milk and protects mucosal surfaces rather than crossing the placenta efficiently.
notes.C: IgM is usually a large pentamer in serum and does not normally cross the placenta by this route.
notes.D: IgD is most familiar as a surface receptor on B cells and is not the major transferred antibody.
notes.E: IgE binds mast cell Fc receptors and is not the usual class providing placentally transferred systemic protection.

questions.stem: Which class predominates in a primary antibody response before class switching?
questions.why: Newly activated naïve B cells can secrete IgM before changing heavy-chain constant regions. Later switching can generate other isotypes without changing the original antigen specificity.

notes.A: IgE generally requires isotype switching driven by appropriate helper signals rather than being the usual first secreted class.
notes.B: IgA is prominent in mucosal secretions and generally appears after class switching.
notes.C: IgD is commonly coexpressed on naïve B cells but is not usually the predominant early secreted class.
notes.D: IgG can become abundant after class switching and is often prominent in secondary responses.

questions.stem: Which structural form best describes secreted serum IgM?
questions.why: Most secreted serum IgM consists of five basic units joined with a J chain. Their multiple binding sites give high avidity, and bound IgM is effective at activating classical complement.

notes.A: Membrane IgM is monomeric on a B cell, while serum IgM is usually assembled into a larger polymer.
notes.B: A dimer is the usual form of secretory IgA rather than the predominant circulating form of IgM.
notes.D: Three basic units do not describe the usual J-chain-containing secreted IgM structure.
notes.E: A tetramer is not the typical circulating arrangement, although structural forms can vary.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is predominant in mucosal secretions and colostrum?
questions.why: Secretory IgA is abundant at mucosal surfaces and in colostrum. Its secretory component helps protect it from degradation, allowing it to limit microbial attachment at epithelial surfaces.

notes.B: IgD is mainly a naïve B-cell surface receptor and is not the predominant secretory antibody.
notes.C: Serum IgM is important for early systemic responses, though polymeric IgM can also appear in secretions.
notes.D: IgE typically acts through Fc receptors on mast cells and is not the main antibody in colostrum.
notes.E: IgG is abundant in serum, but epithelial transport of dimeric IgA predominates in most mucosal secretions.

questions.stem: Which components are characteristic of secretory dimeric IgA?
questions.why: The J chain joins two IgA units and helps them bind the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor. After epithelial passage, a portion of that receptor remains attached as the secretory component.

notes.A: Gamma denotes an IgG heavy chain and CD3 is a T-cell signalling complex rather than part of secretory IgA.
notes.B: Fibrinogen acts in coagulation and complement proteins can support immunity, but neither forms the IgA dimer.
notes.C: Alpha-2-macroglobulin binds certain proteases and C3b is an opsonin rather than a component of secretory IgA.
notes.E: Perforin and granzymes are cytotoxic granule proteins, not structural elements of a mucosal antibody.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is strongly linked to immediate allergy and helminth defence?
questions.why: IgE binds high-affinity receptors on mast cells and basophils. Antigen-dependent activation can trigger immediate allergy, and related type 2 responses contribute to defence against parasitic worms.

notes.A: IgD mainly serves as a surface antigen receptor on naïve B cells rather than arming mast cells.
notes.C: IgG has major roles in opsonisation and neutralisation but is not the classic immunoglobulin driving immediate allergic degranulation.
notes.D: IgA primarily promotes immune exclusion at mucosal surfaces rather than binding high-affinity IgE receptors on mast cells.
notes.E: IgM is an early antibody and an effective complement activator rather than the characteristic class in immediate allergy.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is commonly expressed as an antigen receptor on mature naïve B cells?
questions.why: Mature naïve B cells typically coexpress surface IgM and IgD with the same antigen specificity. Alternative RNA processing produces the two heavy-chain constant regions without class switching.

notes.A: IgE usually appears after class switching and is not the characteristic receptor on a mature naïve cell.
notes.B: Surface IgA marks some antigen-experienced cells after switching, rather than the usual pre-activation IgM and IgD pattern.
notes.C: IgG4 is a switched IgG subclass and is not the usual naïve receptor class.
notes.D: Secretory IgA is released at mucosal surfaces and is different from an unswitched B-cell surface receptor.

questions.stem: A toxin is rendered unable to bind its host-cell receptor by a specific antibody. Which mechanism is illustrated?
questions.why: A neutralising antibody binds a toxin in a way that blocks its interaction with the host-cell receptor. It can prevent the toxin from acting without relying on direct killing of a cell.

notes.A: Agglutination links particles into clumps, rather than specifically blocking a soluble toxin's receptor-binding interaction.
notes.B: Opsonisation coats a target for phagocytic recognition, which is a different consequence from directly preventing receptor binding.
notes.D: Fibrinolysis breaks down fibrin clots and is unrelated to antibody blocking of a toxin.
notes.E: Clonal deletion removes selected lymphocytes during tolerance and does not directly block a toxin from attaching.

questions.stem: Which term describes an antibody's overall multivalent binding strength?
questions.why: Avidity is the combined strength of several binding contacts between an antibody and its target. It depends on intrinsic site affinity, how many sites engage and their arrangement.

notes.B: Affinity is the strength of a single binding-site interaction, rather than the combined effect of multiple contacts.
notes.C: Valence refers to the number of binding sites or determinants, which can influence overall binding strength.
notes.D: Isotype denotes an antibody's constant-region class rather than the combined strength of its contacts.
notes.E: Allotype refers to an inherited immunoglobulin variant, rather than how strongly multiple sites bind.

questions.stem: Which term describes strength between one epitope and one antibody combining site?
questions.why: Affinity describes the intrinsic strength of the interaction between a single antibody combining site and its epitope. It can be expressed through the equilibrium dissociation constant.

notes.A: Avidity combines the effects of multiple binding interactions and their positions rather than measuring one site alone.
notes.B: Isotype classifies immunoglobulin constant regions, which often determine effector properties rather than site affinity.
notes.C: Allotype describes inherited allelic differences in immunoglobulin structure rather than binding strength.
notes.E: Valence counts potential binding sites, rather than measuring the strength with which one site binds.

questions.stem: Which complement pathway is typically initiated when C1q binds antigen-bound IgG or IgM?
questions.why: C1q recognises accessible Fc regions in certain antibodies after they bind antigen. This activates the C1 enzymes and starts the classical complement cascade.

notes.A: The alternative pathway uses C3 activation and factors B and D without requiring C1q to attach to antibodies.
notes.C: The lectin pathway starts when recognition proteins such as mannose-binding lectin bind carbohydrates rather than antibody Fc.
notes.D: The kallikrein pathway is part of the plasma contact system, not the C1q-triggered complement pathway.
notes.E: Fibrinolysis breaks down fibrin clots rather than transmitting an antibody-dependent C1 activation signal.

questions.stem: Which complement activation pathway is initiated by mannose-binding lectin on microbes?
questions.why: Mannose-binding lectin recognises patterns of sugars on microbial surfaces. Its associated proteases activate complement by cleaving components that also feed into the classical pathway's C3 convertase.

notes.A: Classical initiation usually uses C1q recognition of clustered antibody Fc rather than mannose-binding lectin.
notes.B: The alternative pathway amplifies C3b deposition through factors B and D instead of being initiated by lectin binding.
notes.C: The contact pathway involves factor XII and related coagulation proteins rather than mannose-binding lectin.
notes.D: Fibrinolytic enzymes remove fibrin and are separate from the recognition step of lectin complement activation.

questions.stem: Which complement fragment most directly promotes phagocytosis by coating microorganisms?
questions.why: C3 cleavage generates C3b, which can attach to a microbial surface. Complement receptors on phagocytes recognise deposited C3b or its derivatives, promoting ingestion of the coated organism.

notes.B: C3a is a soluble inflammatory signal and is not the main surface-deposited C3 fragment used for opsonisation.
notes.C: C5a strongly recruits and activates inflammatory cells but does not form the principal opsonic coat.
notes.D: C1q can bind recognition targets in the classical pathway, while C3b is the main downstream complement opsonin.
notes.E: C9 contributes to the terminal membrane pore rather than providing the usual tag for phagocyte uptake.

questions.stem: Which complement split product is a particularly powerful neutrophil chemoattractant?
questions.why: C5a is released when C5 is cleaved, and its concentration gradient can recruit neutrophils. It also activates inflammatory responses and is a potent anaphylatoxin.

notes.A: C3b mainly attaches to surfaces for opsonisation rather than serving as the potent soluble attractant.
notes.B: C1q recognises targets to initiate classical activation rather than providing the C5-derived neutrophil signal.
notes.C: C4b is a deposited component of classical or lectin convertase, not the major soluble neutrophil chemoattractant.
notes.E: C9 assembles in terminal membrane pores and does not direct neutrophil migration.

questions.stem: Which complement components assemble into the membrane attack complex?
questions.why: C5b recruits C6 and C7 to form a membrane-associated complex. C8 inserts into the membrane before C9 assembles. Multiple C9 molecules complete the terminal pore.

notes.A: C1q and C4 participate in classical activation and early convertase assembly rather than forming the terminal pore.
notes.C: C2 and C4 fragments help form the classical and lectin C3 convertase, upstream of membrane attack.
notes.D: C3a and C5a act as soluble inflammatory mediators and do not assemble into the membrane attack complex.
notes.E: Factors B and D help form the alternative pathway convertase rather than joining the terminal membrane pore.

questions.stem: Which C3 convertase is formed by the classical and lectin complement pathways?
questions.why: Classical and lectin activation cleave C4 and C2 to assemble C4b2a on a surface. This complex cleaves C3 into soluble C3a and surface-binding C3b.

notes.A: C3bBb is the alternative pathway C3 convertase, using factor B rather than the C4 and C2 components.
notes.B: C5b–9 is the assembled terminal membrane attack complex and does not function as the C3-cleaving enzyme.
notes.C: The C1 complex recognises classical pathway targets and starts early proteolysis, before C3 convertase is formed.
notes.D: C3a and C5a are inflammatory cleavage products rather than the protease complex that acts on C3.

questions.stem: What is the predominant protective purpose of complement opsonization?

options.label: C
options.text: Converting all IgA molecules into IgG

options.label: E
options.text: Generating a fibrin clot without thrombin

questions.why: Complement opsonisation coats a microbial surface with products such as C3b and iC3b. Phagocyte receptors bind these deposited fragments and help the phagocyte ingest the tagged microbe.

notes.B: T-cell receptor rearrangement occurs in developing T cells and is not regulated by coating a microbe with complement.
notes.C: Antibody class switching is a B-cell process and is separate from complement-mediated uptake of a target.
notes.D: Complement can damage host cells when poorly regulated, but the protective purpose of opsonisation is microbial clearance.
notes.E: Fibrin clotting depends on coagulation enzymes, while complement opsonisation marks a target for immune uptake.

questions.stem: A deficiency in terminal complement components most directly impairs which function?

options.label: B
options.text: Processing of peptides for MHC II

options.label: C
options.text: Release of cytokines by plasma cells

questions.why: Late complement components from C5b to C9 form the terminal membrane attack complex. A deficiency impairs lytic pore formation and particularly increases susceptibility to invasive Neisseria infections.

notes.A: B-cell maturation takes place mainly in bone marrow and does not require assembly of the terminal complement pore.
notes.B: MHC class II processing uses intracellular proteolysis and loading, not the terminal complement components.
notes.C: Plasma cells chiefly secrete antibodies, a separate function from lysis by the membrane attack complex.
notes.E: Switching to IgA depends on B-cell signals and DNA recombination, rather than on terminal pore formation.

questions.stem: A cytokine acts on the same cell that secreted it. Which pattern of signalling is this?
questions.why: Autocrine signalling occurs when the secreting cell also has receptors for its own cytokine. This can reinforce that cell's activation or help regulate the duration of its response.

notes.A: A paracrine signal acts chiefly on neighbouring cells rather than returning to the same secreting cell.
notes.C: Endocrine signalling relies on a circulating messenger to act at a distant site.
notes.D: Juxtacrine signalling requires direct cell contact or a membrane-bound interaction rather than soluble signalling to the same cell.
notes.E: Neurocrine release refers to signalling from neurons, rather than defining a cytokine acting back on its producer.

questions.stem: A cytokine acts mainly on nearby cells in the tissue. Which pattern of signalling is illustrated?
questions.why: A paracrine cytokine diffuses a short distance from its source to nearby target cells. It can therefore coordinate local tissue responses without requiring transport through the circulation.

notes.A: In autocrine signalling the releasing cell responds to its own messenger rather than acting mainly on neighbours.
notes.B: Endocrine signalling involves transport over longer distances, typically in the circulation.
notes.C: Intracrine signalling acts within the cell producing the signal, instead of diffusing to neighbouring cells.
notes.D: Neurocrine describes signals released by neurons and does not define local diffusion of cytokines between tissue cells.

questions.stem: One cytokine triggers different biological effects in several cell types. This property is called:
questions.why: Pleiotropy describes one cytokine producing different responses in different target cells. Receptor expression and downstream signalling programmes can vary between those cells.

notes.A: Redundancy means different cytokines can produce a similar response, rather than one cytokine having several effects.
notes.B: Antagonism occurs when one signal diminishes another signal's effect, not simply when cell types respond differently.
notes.D: Synergy involves combined cytokine effects rather than the range of responses elicited by an individual cytokine.
notes.E: Chemotaxis describes directed movement along a gradient, which is only one possible effect.

questions.stem: Two different cytokines stimulate the same biological effect. Which property is illustrated?
questions.why: Cytokine redundancy means distinct signals can produce overlapping biological outcomes. This can preserve a function even when one of the cytokines that normally supports it is absent.

notes.B: Pleiotropy is the converse pattern: one cytokine has multiple effects on different cell populations.
notes.C: Antagonism occurs when one cytokine opposes or dampens another rather than both producing the same outcome.
notes.D: Chemotaxis is a directional motility response, not a term for cytokines with overlapping effects.
notes.E: Tolerance is reduced responsiveness to an antigen and does not describe two cytokines sharing a function.

questions.stem: Two cytokines together produce a stronger effect than either alone. Their interaction is:
questions.why: Synergy describes cooperative enhancement of biological action.

questions.stem: Which chemokine is particularly associated with attracting neutrophils?
questions.why: CXCL8 recruits neutrophils by activating chemokine receptors and guiding them along a concentration gradient. This is a major component of many acute inflammatory responses.

notes.A: CCL2 mainly recruits monocytes rather than serving as the classic acute neutrophil chemoattractant.
notes.C: CXCL12 helps regulate cell homing and marrow retention through CXCR4, rather than being the textbook neutrophil signal.
notes.D: CCL5 recruits targets such as T cells and eosinophils rather than being the principal chemokine identified here.
notes.E: CXCL10 is associated with recruitment of activated lymphocytes through CXCR3, rather than classic neutrophil recruitment.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is important for T-cell proliferation after activation?
questions.why: Activated T cells can produce IL-2 and increase expression of its high-affinity receptor. This signal promotes clonal expansion and supports differentiation after the initial antigen response.

notes.A: IL-4 promotes type 2 differentiation and can support particular class-switching pathways rather than being the principal T-cell growth factor.
notes.B: IL-5 supports eosinophil development and activation rather than driving the main clonal expansion signal in activated T cells.
notes.C: IL-8 is a chemokine for neutrophil recruitment rather than the T-cell autocrine growth signal.
notes.D: IL-10 generally limits inflammatory activation rather than serving as the classical cytokine for activated T-cell proliferation.

questions.stem: Which cytokine strongly activates macrophage microbicidal functions during Th1 responses?
questions.why: Th1 cells can release interferon gamma, which signals macrophages to increase antimicrobial functions. It is particularly important for controlling some microbes that survive inside phagocytes.

notes.A: IL-4 supports type 2 responses and can promote alternative macrophage activation rather than the classical Th1 pattern.
notes.B: IL-5 promotes eosinophil responses rather than strongly inducing the classic Th1 macrophage programme.
notes.D: IL-8 drives neutrophil recruitment, rather than being the hallmark cytokine for Th1-dependent macrophage activation.
notes.E: IL-10 can suppress macrophage inflammatory and antigen-presenting functions rather than activating the classic microbicidal response.

questions.stem: Which pair is especially associated with early antiviral signalling by infected cells?
questions.why: Interferon alpha and interferon beta are type I interferons that signal after viral recognition. They induce antiviral gene expression in infected and nearby cells early in the response.

notes.B: IL-4 and IL-5 are associated with type 2 immunity, rather than the early virus-induced type I interferon response.
notes.C: IL-2 and IL-7 regulate T-cell growth or survival, rather than constituting the early type I interferon pair.
notes.D: IL-10 and TGF-beta often limit or regulate inflammation rather than producing the prototypical antiviral interferon signal.
notes.E: TNF-alpha and IL-6 are important inflammatory cytokines but do not make up the type I interferon pair.

questions.stem: Severe infection causes macrophages to release cytokines linked to fever, capillary leakage and shock. Which pair is key?
questions.why: Activated macrophages can release TNF-alpha and IL-1 during severe infection. Excess systemic signalling contributes to fever and endothelial activation, while vascular leak and altered tone can contribute to shock.

notes.A: IL-4 and IL-5 mainly coordinate type 2 inflammation and eosinophil-associated responses rather than being the classic pair driving shock.
notes.B: IL-2 and IL-7 support lymphocyte proliferation and survival, unlike the named mediators of acute systemic inflammation.
notes.C: IFN-gamma activates macrophages, while IL-10 often constrains inflammatory signalling rather than forming the classic fever and shock pair.
notes.E: IL-13 contributes to type 2 immunity and IL-17 supports inflammatory cell recruitment, but neither defines the classic pair.

questions.stem: A defect in the common gamma-chain cytokine receptor can cause which condition?
questions.why: The IL2RG protein is a shared receptor chain for multiple cytokines, including those needed for T-cell and NK-cell development. Loss of its function can cause X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency.

notes.A: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia involves immune destruction of red cells, not the typical congenital failure of lymphocyte development.
notes.C: Haemophilia A is caused by factor VIII deficiency rather than by impaired common gamma-chain cytokine signalling.
notes.D: Familial hypercholesterolaemia involves defective LDL clearance rather than a shared receptor defect in developing lymphocytes.
notes.E: Hereditary angioedema commonly involves abnormal control of bradykinin, separate from common gamma-chain signalling.

questions.stem: Defective IFN-γ receptor signalling particularly predisposes to infection with:
questions.why: Interferon gamma receptor signalling helps macrophages control intracellular mycobacteria. Defects can therefore cause a marked susceptibility to mycobacterial infections, including otherwise relatively weak organisms.

notes.A: Helminth defence often involves type 2 responses and eosinophils rather than relying primarily on the macrophage IFN-gamma pathway.
notes.B: Early control of many respiratory viruses relies strongly on type I interferons, distinct from the IFN-gamma susceptibility described here.
notes.C: Chronic mucocutaneous Candida susceptibility is more closely linked to impaired IL-17 immunity than to this classic receptor defect.
notes.D: Malaria immunity includes multiple responses, but the characteristic susceptibility in this defect is to mycobacteria.

questions.stem: Which receptor-signalling mechanism is characteristic of many class I and II cytokine receptors?
questions.why: Many class I and II cytokine receptors signal through associated Janus kinases, which phosphorylate STAT proteins. Activated STATs enter the nucleus and help regulate transcription.

notes.A: Wnt signalling can stabilise beta-catenin, but it is not the canonical route from these cytokine receptors.
notes.B: Nuclear steroid receptors bind lipid-soluble hormones and directly regulate transcription rather than using receptor-associated JAKs.
notes.D: DNA repair pathways respond to genomic damage rather than relaying this extracellular cytokine signal.
notes.E: Thromboxane signals through a G-protein-coupled receptor in platelet activation, separate from JAK–STAT signalling.

questions.stem: A biologic drug neutralizes TNF-α in rheumatoid arthritis. Which biological consequence is intended?
questions.why: TNF-alpha can amplify inflammatory activity in rheumatoid arthritis. Neutralising it reduces signalling through its receptors and lowers downstream inflammatory responses in affected tissues.

notes.B: Fibrinogen cross-linking involves coagulation enzymes and is not the intended target of anti-TNF therapy.
notes.C: T-cell receptor rearrangement occurs during lymphocyte development rather than being an intended consequence of TNF neutralisation.
notes.D: Vitamin K recycling supports clotting factor synthesis, which is separate from the TNF receptor pathway.
notes.E: Eosinophil degranulation is associated chiefly with type 2 pathways and is not the intended effect of TNF blockade.

questions.stem: Which immune mechanism is especially important during the earliest stages of many viral infections?
questions.why: Type I interferons can be produced early after cells detect viral material. Their signalling induces an antiviral state before a new antigen-specific lymphocyte response has fully developed.

notes.A: IgE production generally involves class switching and is associated more with allergy and type 2 immune responses.
notes.B: Germinal-centre affinity maturation is part of a later adaptive B-cell response after activation.
notes.C: Antibody memory can matter on re-exposure, but new memory is not the usual first response to a novel infection.
notes.D: Antigen-driven expansion of cytotoxic T cells usually takes longer than innate type I interferon signalling.

questions.stem: Which adaptive immune cell directly kills virus-infected cells displaying viral peptides on MHC class I?
questions.why: A cytotoxic CD8 T cell recognises a suitable peptide–MHC class I complex on the infected cell. The activated effector can trigger apoptosis through cytotoxic granules or death-receptor signalling.

notes.A: Conventional CD4 helper T cells chiefly recognise MHC class II and support immune activation rather than performing the usual class-I-restricted killing.
notes.C: Mature B cells recognise antigen and can differentiate into antibody-secreting cells rather than directly killing through peptide–MHC I.
notes.D: Plasma cells are differentiated antibody-secreting cells and do not perform the CD8 T-cell killing response.
notes.E: Follicular dendritic cells display native antigen to B cells in follicles rather than killing class-I-bearing infected cells.

questions.stem: For defence against extracellular pyogenic bacteria, which antibody function is particularly useful?
questions.why: Opsonising IgG can bind to bacterial surfaces, leaving Fc exposed to receptors on phagocytes. Complement deposition can add recognition sites, improving ingestion of extracellular bacteria.

notes.A: Cytotoxic T-cell killing targets infected host cells and is not an antibody-mediated route of bacterial uptake.
notes.B: Type I interferon production primarily establishes antiviral responses rather than tagging extracellular pyogenic bacteria.
notes.C: Intracellular peptide processing helps antigen presentation, not the direct coating of extracellular targets for phagocytes.
notes.E: The thymic medulla supports T-cell development and tolerance rather than functioning as an antibody effector.

questions.stem: Why are encapsulated bacteria sometimes difficult for phagocytes to clear?
questions.why: A bacterial capsule can make surface recognition and engulfment less efficient. Antibody and complement can improve recognition by phagocytes, helping overcome that barrier to clearance.

notes.B: IgA is made by host plasma cells, rather than being synthesised by a bacterial capsule.
notes.C: Capsules can impede ingestion, but they do not eliminate all neutrophils or account for so broad an effect.
notes.D: T-cell receptors are made by host lymphocytes rather than being expressed by a bacterial capsule.
notes.E: A capsule can impair uptake without preventing all cytokine signalling by host immune cells.

questions.stem: Which secretory antibody helps prevent bacterial attachment to mucosal epithelium?
questions.why: Secretory IgA binds microbes and their products in mucosal secretions. By limiting adhesion to epithelial surfaces it supports immune exclusion without requiring strong local inflammation.

notes.A: IgD is chiefly a naïve B-cell surface receptor rather than the main antibody coating mucosal surfaces.
notes.B: IgE binds mast-cell receptors and participates in immediate allergy and helminth responses rather than routine mucosal exclusion.
notes.D: IgG4 is a serum IgG subclass and is not the standard predominant secretory antibody at mucosal sites.
notes.E: Secretory IgM can contribute to mucosal defence, but IgA is the predominant specialised antibody there.

questions.stem: Which response is particularly important against intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Direct action of platelet factor IV

questions.why: Th1 cells release interferon gamma and promote macrophage activation in tuberculosis. This improves control of mycobacteria residing within macrophages, where circulating antibodies have limited access.

notes.A: IgE and eosinophils are more characteristic of type 2 responses against parasites outside host cells.
notes.B: Mucosal IgA can block attachment at epithelial surfaces, but it cannot substitute for control of organisms inside macrophages.
notes.C: Mast-cell histamine supports acute inflammatory and allergic responses rather than providing the critical intracellular macrophage programme.
notes.D: Platelet factor IV is linked to platelet biology and does not provide the main Th1-mediated defence.

questions.stem: A mutation produces a small progressive alteration in an influenza surface antigen. Which process is illustrated?
questions.why: Antigenic drift is the gradual accumulation of small changes that can alter recognition of influenza surface antigens. Existing immunity may therefore recognise later variants less well.

notes.A: Antigenic shift is an abrupt major antigenic change, rather than the gradual process described.
notes.C: Class switching alters the constant region of a host antibody and does not change a viral antigen.
notes.D: Clonal deletion is a mechanism of host lymphocyte tolerance rather than accumulation of changes in influenza.
notes.E: Complement fixation is an immune effector process, not the name for gradual change in an antigen.

questions.stem: A major reassortment of influenza genome segments creates a markedly new surface-antigen combination. This represents:
questions.why: Antigenic shift is an abrupt major change in influenza A surface antigens. Natural changes of this kind are distinct from the smaller changes that accumulate during seasonal antigenic drift.

notes.A: Drift describes gradual antigenic changes rather than the abrupt emergence of a substantially different antigen pattern.
notes.B: Affinity maturation changes how strongly host antibodies bind antigen rather than changing the influenza antigen itself.
notes.C: Antibody gene recombination occurs in host B cells and is distinct from natural changes in an influenza genome.
notes.E: V(D)J rearrangement creates receptor diversity in developing lymphocytes rather than causing abrupt influenza antigen change.

questions.stem: Which mechanism is implicated in antibody-dependent enhancement during some dengue infections?

options.label: A
options.text: Fc receptor uptake of virus–IgG complexes

options.label: B
options.text: Destruction of MHC I by activated platelets

options.label: C
options.text: Prevention of virus binding by neutralizing IgA

options.label: D
options.text: Complement-mediated lysis of all infected cells

questions.why: In some dengue infections, pre-existing antibodies bind without neutralising the virus effectively. Fc receptors can take up these complexes, which can contribute to more severe disease.

notes.B: Activated platelets have roles in haemostasis and inflammation rather than driving the antibody-dependent Fc receptor pathway.
notes.C: Neutralising IgA would block attachment and protect the host rather than explain antibody-dependent enhancement.
notes.D: Complement can contribute to immune responses, but enhancement here involves Fc receptor uptake of antibody-bound material.
notes.E: Class-switch recombination alters host immunoglobulin genes and does not occur in dengue viral genomes.

questions.stem: A helminth infection triggers IgE production and eosinophil recruitment. Which helper T-cell pattern is most typical?
questions.why: Th2 cells produce cytokines such as IL-4 and IL-5. These support IgE-associated responses and eosinophil recruitment or activation, a pattern typical of defence against many helminths.

notes.A: Th1 responses use interferon gamma to activate macrophages, particularly against many intracellular microbes.
notes.B: Th17 cells can promote neutrophil responses to some extracellular bacteria and fungi rather than driving the classic IgE response.
notes.D: Regulatory T cells restrain immune activation and do not characteristically drive IgE and eosinophil responses.
notes.E: Cytotoxic CD8 cells kill selected target cells and are distinct from the helper programme associated with helminths.

questions.stem: A protozoan lives mainly inside macrophages. Which protective response is most likely needed?
questions.why: Th1-associated interferon gamma can activate macrophages and increase their ability to control organisms already inside them. This addresses the intracellular location of the protozoan.

notes.A: Secretory IgD in bronchial mucus is not the characteristic defence against organisms residing within macrophages.
notes.B: Platelet aggregation forms a haemostatic plug and does not provide the principal antimicrobial response inside macrophages.
notes.C: IgE-associated responses are more useful against some large extracellular parasites than against protozoa inside macrophages.
notes.D: Fibrin formation limits bleeding but does not replace cytokine-driven activation of an infected macrophage.

questions.stem: Which physical defence limits pathogen survival after entry into the stomach?
questions.why: Gastric acid creates a low-pH environment that reduces survival of many swallowed organisms. It is a nonspecific chemical barrier that acts before an antigen-specific immune response is needed.

notes.A: IgE chiefly acts through mast cells and basophils and is not the principal antimicrobial property of gastric juice.
notes.C: Circulating T cells participate in adaptive responses rather than suppressing organisms inside the stomach lumen by acidity.
notes.D: C9 helps form complement pores, but gastric acid is the main luminal barrier identified here.
notes.E: Intestinal MHC class I presents peptides to CD8 T cells and does not establish the low pH of the stomach.

questions.stem: Which inflammatory consequence is associated with high systemic TNF-α release in severe bacterial sepsis?
questions.why: Excess systemic TNF-alpha contributes to inflammatory endothelial activation during severe sepsis. Increased vascular permeability and altered vascular tone can reduce effective circulating volume and lower blood pressure.

notes.A: Bone collagen synthesis is a matrix-building process rather than the immediate circulatory effect of excess TNF-alpha.
notes.B: Endothelial permeability often increases during severe systemic inflammation, allowing fluid to leave the vasculature.
notes.C: Red-cell oxygen affinity is governed mainly by haemoglobin properties and local conditions, rather than this cytokine-mediated leak.
notes.E: Coagulation and platelets may be affected in sepsis, but the characteristic systemic finding includes leaky vessels and hypotension.

questions.stem: A bacterial pathogen secretes an IgA protease. Which defence is most directly weakened?
questions.why: Secretory IgA normally protects mucosa by binding microbial surfaces and limiting attachment. If that antibody is cleaved, the mucosal barrier loses some of its antibody-dependent protection.

notes.B: MHC class I assembly occurs inside host cells and is separate from the actions of secretory antibodies on mucosal surfaces.
notes.C: Thymic positive selection concerns recognition of self MHC by developing T cells, rather than luminal mucosal protection.
notes.D: Macrophages can generate nitric oxide in innate defence, a pathway distinct from secretory IgA activity.
notes.E: Granzymes are cytotoxic lymphocyte effectors and are not the same defence as secretory IgA on an epithelial surface.

questions.stem: Which immune pathway can explain kidney injury from deposition of circulating antigen–antibody complexes?
questions.why: Soluble antigen–antibody complexes can lodge in glomeruli and activate complement locally. Recruitment of inflammatory cells then damages tissue, forming a classic immune complex-mediated pattern.

notes.A: T-cell receptor rearrangement occurs during lymphocyte development rather than explaining inflammatory deposits in glomeruli.
notes.B: Fc-epsilon receptor desensitisation affects IgE-mediated mast-cell responses, not the deposition of circulating complexes.
notes.D: Keratin production supports some epithelial structures and is unrelated to immune complex deposition and complement activation.
notes.E: Vitamin K recycling supports coagulation factor function and does not produce antibody–antigen deposits in the kidney.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between plasma and serum used for laboratory tests?
questions.why: Serum is the liquid remaining after blood clots and the clot is removed. Plasma comes from anticoagulated blood and therefore retains fibrinogen and other clotting components.

notes.A: Plasma contains immunoglobulins, many of which are also present in serum after clotting.
notes.B: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin during clotting, so intact fibrinogen is largely absent from serum.
notes.C: Albumin is a soluble protein present in both plasma and serum and does not distinguish them.
notes.D: Much of the platelet material is trapped in the clot, so separated serum is not a preparation of functional platelets.

questions.stem: What does an antibody titre report in a serial dilution test?

options.label: C
options.text: Total mass of albumin in the sample

options.label: D
options.text: Amount of free complement in plasma

questions.why: An antibody titre is conventionally the reciprocal of the greatest dilution at which a defined reaction is still detectable. It reports a dilution endpoint rather than a directly weighed amount of antibody.

notes.A: The endpoint is the highest dilution still meeting the assay criterion, rather than the lowest dilution showing haemolysis.
notes.C: Albumin measurement reports a different serum protein and is not the dilution endpoint for an antibody reaction.
notes.D: Complement may participate in some assays, but the antibody titre describes how far the sample can be diluted.
notes.E: Initial pH is an assay condition, while titre is an observed endpoint of the dilution series.

questions.stem: A highly sensitive assay is particularly useful because it tends to minimize:
questions.why: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the target condition who test positive. If that proportion is high, fewer affected people are missed and classified as negative.

notes.A: False positives occur among unaffected people and their frequency is chiefly related to specificity.
notes.B: True positives are detected cases and increase as the test detects a larger proportion of affected individuals.
notes.C: True negatives are the unaffected people correctly identified and are associated with test specificity.
notes.E: Cross-reactivity can affect assay specificity, while high sensitivity specifically limits missed cases.

questions.stem: A highly specific diagnostic assay is particularly useful because it tends to minimize:
questions.why: Specificity is the proportion of people without the condition who are correctly identified as negative. Higher specificity therefore gives fewer positive results among unaffected people.

notes.B: False negatives occur among affected people and are chiefly determined by sensitivity.
notes.C: True positives are correctly detected affected individuals and are used to calculate sensitivity rather than specificity.
notes.D: True negatives are the desired correct results among unaffected people and increase with higher specificity.
notes.E: Detection of a target when truly present is generally desirable, rather than something a specific test is meant to minimise.

questions.stem: Why can undiluted serum with extremely high antibody concentration give a falsely weak precipitation reaction?
questions.why: In the prozone, excess antibody saturates available antigen sites without efficiently bridging antigen molecules. Diluting the antibody can restore proportions that allow a visible precipitating lattice.

notes.A: The postzone occurs with excess antigen, which is the opposite imbalance from the one in this specimen.
notes.B: Equivalence supports cross-linking and maximal precipitation rather than a falsely weak result.
notes.D: Precipitation can occur through direct antigen–antibody cross-linking and does not require complement to make the lattice.
notes.E: Enzyme inhibition affects some assay signals, but this pattern is explained by the proportions of antigen and antibody.

questions.stem: A precipitin reaction is weak because the specimen contains far more antigen than antibody. This condition is:
questions.why: A postzone effect occurs when antigen greatly exceeds available antibody. Individual binding events still take place, but there are too few antibody bridges to form large visible complexes.

notes.A: The prozone is a weak reaction caused by antibody excess, whereas this sample has antigen excess.
notes.B: The equivalence zone permits efficient cross-linking and is usually where precipitation is strongest.
notes.C: Increasing avidity can reflect stronger multivalent binding, but the weak result in the stem is caused by reagent proportions.
notes.D: Complement exhaustion does not determine whether a direct antigen–antibody precipitating lattice can form.

questions.stem: Maximum visible precipitation of soluble antigen and antibody usually occurs in which region?
questions.why: At equivalence, available antigen and antibody sites are balanced enough for extensive cross-linking. Large insoluble lattices form more readily than when either reactant is in marked excess.

notes.A: Excess antibody can saturate epitopes without bridging many antigens, weakening visible precipitation.
notes.C: Excess antigen can occupy binding sites without producing sufficiently large cross-linked complexes.
notes.D: The prozone corresponds to antibody excess and typically gives less precipitation than the equivalence zone.
notes.E: The postzone corresponds to antigen excess, which limits lattice formation instead of maximising it.

questions.stem: Which reaction is most appropriate for visibly clumping antibody-coated particulate cells?
questions.why: Agglutination occurs when multivalent binding forms bridges between particles or cells. Those bridges generate visible clumps, rather than the precipitate formed from originally soluble antigen.

notes.A: Precipitation forms insoluble lattices from soluble antigens and is distinguished from visible clumping of particles.
notes.B: Neutralisation blocks a biological interaction such as toxin attachment without requiring visible groups of cells.
notes.C: Opsonisation enhances phagocyte recognition by coating a target rather than necessarily forming visible clumps.
notes.E: Dialysis separates molecules across a membrane and does not depend on antibody bridges between cells.

questions.stem: Which technique relies on an enzyme-linked reagent to produce a measurable colour signal?
questions.why: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays use an enzyme reporter and chromogenic or other detectable substrate.

questions.stem: Which assay directly uses a radionuclide label as part of its detection system?
questions.why: Radioimmunoassay uses a radionuclide-labelled tracer as part of an antigen–antibody measurement. The readout is radioactivity associated with a bound or free fraction.

notes.A: Enzyme immunoassays detect enzyme activity through a reporter reaction rather than using a radionuclide tracer.
notes.B: Immunofluorescence relies on a fluorophore emitting light after excitation rather than counting radioactive decay.
notes.D: Agglutination can be detected by visible clumping and does not inherently require a labelled radionuclide.
notes.E: Typical lateral-flow assays use visible particles or another optical reporter rather than requiring a radioactive tracer.

questions.stem: What best distinguishes avidity from affinity in antibody–antigen binding?
questions.why: Affinity describes binding strength for one antigen–antibody contact. Avidity describes the combined stability when multiple contacts form together and can remain engaged despite release at one site.

notes.A: Fab and Fc describe antibody regions, whereas affinity and avidity describe binding interactions.
notes.B: Both terms apply to binding and do not distinguish activation of the innate immune system from the adaptive system.
notes.C: Serum and plasma are sample types, and either can contain antibodies whose binding has affinity and avidity.
notes.D: Protein manufacture and transport do not define the difference between the strength of one contact and combined binding.

questions.stem: Antibodies against a related species produce a positive serological result. Which limitation best explains it?
questions.why: Antibodies can recognise similar or shared epitopes on antigens from related organisms. A serological assay can therefore react with a related species even in the absence of the target infection.

notes.A: High specificity would tend to exclude such reactions rather than explain a positive result to a related antigen.
notes.C: Binding to the related species shows that an antigenic determinant is still recognised by the antibody.
notes.D: A serum reaction based on antibody requires immunoglobulin to be present, even if its target is cross-reactive.
notes.E: A cross-reaction requires some affinity for the shared epitope, rather than a complete absence of binding.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes active immunity obtained by routine vaccination?

options.label: A
options.text: Preformed antibody is supplied from a donor

options.label: B
options.text: The host is protected only by innate barriers

options.label: C
options.text: Protective antibodies arise from donor plasma

options.label: D
options.text: Host lymphocytes produce the protective response

options.label: E
options.text: The vaccine directly digests circulating microbes

questions.why: Routine vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen or instructions for producing it. The recipient's own lymphocytes respond and can persist as memory cells, producing active immunity.

notes.A: Donor antibodies confer passive immunity because the recipient receives the protective products without making them.
notes.B: Innate mechanisms help initiate the response, but active vaccination depends on adaptive lymphocytes for specificity and memory.
notes.C: Transferred donor plasma provides temporary passive antibodies rather than generating active vaccination responses.
notes.E: Vaccines prime host immune responses and do not act as enzymes that digest microbes in circulation.

questions.stem: Which component of a vaccine primarily supplies the specificity of the immune response?
questions.why: The vaccine antigen contains the structures recognised by specific lymphocytes and their receptors. It determines the target of immune memory, while other ingredients support delivery or stability.

notes.B: An adjuvant strengthens or shapes a response but does not provide the principal antigenic target.
notes.C: A preservative limits contamination in certain formulations rather than defining what lymphocytes recognise.
notes.D: A buffer helps maintain pH during storage and does not determine immunological specificity.
notes.E: A stabiliser protects the formulation from deterioration rather than serving as the main antigenic determinant.

questions.stem: Which vaccine component is included chiefly to enhance immunogenicity?
questions.why: An adjuvant is included to improve the immune response to an antigen. It can enhance innate activation or antigen presentation, supporting a more effective or durable adaptive response.

notes.A: Buffers maintain an appropriate pH and do not primarily serve as immune stimulants.
notes.B: Stabilisers help preserve antigen integrity during storage rather than directly enhancing the immune response to it.
notes.D: Preservatives limit microbial contamination during storage or use rather than acting chiefly as immune enhancers.
notes.E: Diluents restore or adjust the dose's fluid volume and are not the component that principally improves immunogenicity.

questions.stem: Which vaccine component is included chiefly to reduce microbial contamination of multi-dose preparations?
questions.why: A preservative in certain multidose vaccines prevents unintended microbial growth after repeated access to the container. It serves a formulation safety role rather than determining the immune response's specificity.

notes.A: An adjuvant enhances the host response to antigen and is not included principally to inhibit contamination.
notes.B: The antigen provides the immune target rather than protecting a vial against organisms introduced during use.
notes.C: A buffer maintains pH and is distinct from the ingredient chiefly used to prevent microbial growth.
notes.D: A stabiliser preserves the activity of formulation components and is not chiefly intended to prevent contamination.

questions.stem: Why is a toxoid vaccine able to produce protection without causing the toxin's disease?

options.label: E
options.text: It blocks all host antibody responses

questions.why: A toxoid has lost the harmful activity of a toxin but retains enough antigenic structure to induce an immune response. The antibodies generated can neutralise the corresponding active toxin.

notes.A: Retaining recognisable epitopes is necessary to induce antibodies that recognise the active toxin.
notes.C: A toxoid is made inactive, so the preparation does not require a toxin that still has its harmful activity.
notes.D: Toxoid vaccination can produce memory lymphocytes rather than destroying those that respond to the antigen.
notes.E: Induction of antibodies is the protective goal, not a process the toxoid is intended to block.

questions.stem: What is the key aim of linking a bacterial polysaccharide to a carrier protein in a conjugate vaccine?

options.label: A
options.text: Suppress antigen uptake by dendritic cells

options.label: B
options.text: Prevent formation of memory B cells

options.label: D
options.text: Recruit T-cell help for the B-cell response

options.label: E
options.text: Directly kill bacteria in the syringe

questions.why: A B cell that recognises the polysaccharide can present peptides from the linked carrier to helper T cells. The helper signals support class switching and more durable memory.

notes.A: Conjugate vaccination uses antigen processing and presentation to recruit help, rather than suppressing those functions.
notes.B: The added T-cell help generally supports memory B-cell formation instead of preventing it.
notes.C: Class switching can be enhanced, but the response does not require all antibodies to become IgE.
notes.E: The conjugate is an immunogen that primes the host response rather than directly killing organisms in the formulation.

questions.stem: Which vaccine type contains a weakened organism capable of limited replication in the host?
questions.why: A live attenuated vaccine contains a weakened organism that can still replicate to a limited degree. This permits antigen exposure and stimulation of adaptive immunity without the usual disease of natural infection.

notes.B: An inactivated whole-organism vaccine contains organisms that cannot replicate after administration.
notes.C: A subunit preparation contains selected antigens rather than an intact organism capable of limited replication.
notes.D: A toxoid is an inactive antigenic form of a toxin, not a replicating organism.
notes.E: A purified polysaccharide consists of nonliving carbohydrate antigen that cannot multiply in the recipient.

questions.stem: What is the primary immunological purpose of a booster dose?

options.label: E
options.text: Eliminate all existing memory T cells

questions.why: A booster exposes the immune system to the antigen again after priming. Antigen-specific memory cells can respond more rapidly, increasing or renewing the level of protection.

notes.A: Innate cells still contribute to vaccine responses, but a booster does not replace those cell populations.
notes.B: The antigen need only be presented again, rather than persisting permanently in the recipient.
notes.D: A secondary antibody response is commonly amplified after a booster rather than suppressed.
notes.E: Existing memory T cells can be recalled by the booster and are not meant to be eliminated.

questions.stem: Which mechanism defines a classic type I hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: In classic type I hypersensitivity, IgE attaches to high-affinity receptors on mast cells during sensitisation. Re-exposure can cross-link the bound IgE and trigger rapid mediator release.

notes.A: IgG against fixed cell-associated antigen is typical of type II hypersensitivity rather than classic immediate allergy.
notes.B: Soluble immune complex deposition characterises type III hypersensitivity, not mast-cell activation through bound IgE.
notes.C: Delayed T-cell inflammation is a type IV mechanism and usually appears later than immediate IgE-dependent symptoms.
notes.D: Antibody-independent cytotoxicity uses other effector pathways rather than cross-linking IgE on sensitised mast cells.

questions.stem: Which molecule is the principal preformed mediator released rapidly by degranulating mast cells?
questions.why: Histamine is stored in mast-cell granules and can be released rapidly after activation. It contributes to immediate changes in vascular permeability and can contract airway smooth muscle.

notes.A: IL-2 is a cytokine associated with activated T-cell growth, rather than the chief preformed vasoactive granule mediator.
notes.C: C3b is generated by complement cleavage and attaches to surfaces instead of being stored as mast-cell histamine.
notes.D: Perforin is stored in cytotoxic lymphocyte granules and serves a different role in target-cell killing.
notes.E: Fibrinogen is a circulating coagulation protein, rather than a vasoactive mediator released from mast-cell granules.

questions.stem: Which class of hypersensitivity best describes antibody-mediated destruction of transfused red cells?
questions.why: Transfusion reactions can occur when recipient IgM or IgG recognises an antigen fixed on donor red cells. Complement and other effector mechanisms can destroy those cells, fitting type II hypersensitivity.

notes.A: Type I involves IgE-dependent mast-cell activation rather than antibodies targeting red-cell surface antigens for destruction.
notes.B: Type III involves deposition of soluble immune complexes rather than antibody binding directly to the transfused cells.
notes.C: Type IV is driven by sensitised T cells rather than antibodies against red-cell surface antigens.
notes.E: Mechanical or chemical haemolysis can be nonimmune, but this stem explicitly describes antibody-mediated destruction.

questions.stem: Which class of hypersensitivity is characterized by deposition of soluble antigen–antibody complexes?
questions.why: In type III hypersensitivity, soluble antigen and antibody form complexes that are deposited in tissues such as vessel walls or glomeruli. Complement and recruited cells can then cause inflammation.

notes.B: Type I is immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell activation rather than tissue deposition of soluble complexes.
notes.C: Type II targets antigens already fixed to a cell or matrix, rather than complexes formed in solution.
notes.D: Type IV involves antigen-specific T cells and does not depend on antibody complexes for the defining tissue injury.
notes.E: Innate inflammatory pathways can execute injury, but formation of specific antigen–antibody complexes requires an adaptive component.

questions.stem: Which mechanism underlies allergic contact dermatitis from a sensitizing chemical?
questions.why: Sensitising chemicals can generate antigens recognised by T cells after binding to skin proteins. On later exposure, those T cells drive a delayed local inflammatory response in the skin.

notes.A: An IgE-dependent mast-cell reaction is typically immediate rather than the usual delayed reaction to contact sensitisation.
notes.B: IgM-mediated haemolysis targets red cells and represents an antibody-mediated process rather than a skin T-cell response.
notes.D: Circulating immune complexes produce a type III mechanism rather than typical delayed contact dermatitis.
notes.E: Terminal complement pores are not the characteristic cause of the local T-cell inflammation in contact dermatitis.

questions.stem: A tuberculin skin test becomes indurated after roughly 48–72 hours. This is an example of:
questions.why: The skin response reflects sensitised antigen-specific T cells releasing cytokines and recruiting inflammatory cells. This delayed cellular reaction produces induration over roughly 48–72 hours.

notes.A: Type I reactions usually develop rapidly through IgE on mast cells, rather than producing the delayed induration described.
notes.B: Type II reactions involve antibody against fixed cell or matrix structures rather than the tuberculin-specific cellular response.
notes.C: Type III reactions involve tissue deposition of soluble immune complexes, not the main cause of delayed tuberculin induration.
notes.D: The response requires prior antigen sensitisation and is not explained by an immediate nonspecific reaction.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes type II from type III hypersensitivity?

options.label: A
options.text: Type II is driven by IgE while type III uses T cells

options.label: B
options.text: Antibody binds fixed rather than soluble targets

options.label: C
options.text: Type II occurs only in the respiratory epithelium

options.label: D
options.text: Type III requires perforin release by CD8 cells

options.label: E
options.text: Type III has no antibody contribution

questions.why: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibodies binding targets already fixed on cells or tissue matrix. In type III, soluble antigen–antibody complexes form first and can then deposit where they cause inflammation.

notes.A: IgE is typical of type I, while T-cell-driven reactions are type IV rather than the two mechanisms described.
notes.C: Type II injury can occur in blood and other tissues and is not restricted to the respiratory epithelium.
notes.D: CD8 perforin release is a cellular effector process rather than a requirement for soluble complex-mediated injury.
notes.E: Antibodies are essential constituents of type III immune complexes, even though recruited innate cells can produce much of the injury.

questions.stem: A second allergen exposure cross-links mast-cell-bound IgE. Which event is expected immediately?
questions.why: Cross-linking FcεRI-bound IgE triggers mast-cell mediator release during immediate hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: Which cell contributes prominently to many late-phase allergic reactions?
questions.why: Th2 cytokines recruit eosinophils, which contribute to later tissue inflammation.

questions.stem: Which retinal photoreceptors are especially adapted for dim-light vision?
questions.why: Rods are more light-sensitive and mediate scotopic, mainly monochromatic vision.

questions.stem: Which photoreceptors are principally responsible for colour vision in bright light?
questions.why: Cones mediate photopic vision and have different opsins underlying colour discrimination.

questions.stem: Which property makes rods more sensitive than cones in dim light?

options.label: C
options.text: Higher acuity at the foveal centre

options.label: E
options.text: Direct excitation of optic nerve axons

questions.why: Rods respond to low photon intensities, whereas cones require brighter illumination.

questions.stem: Rhodopsin consists of the apoprotein opsin combined with which light-sensitive molecule?
questions.why: The chromophore of dark-adapted rhodopsin is 11-cis-retinal derived from vitamin A.

questions.stem: Which vitamin is the nutritional precursor of the retinal chromophore?
questions.why: Vitamin A supplies retinoids, including retinal required for visual pigment regeneration.

questions.stem: Which symptom is a classic early functional consequence of vitamin A deficiency?
questions.why: Inadequate vitamin A impairs rhodopsin regeneration and causes poor vision in dim light.

questions.stem: Which dietary compound is a provitamin A source from plant foods?
questions.why: Beta-carotene is a carotenoid that can be cleaved to supply vitamin A.
